title: Big Walk fiasco can be a blessing in disguise for AI acceptance
author: Jin_Sakai_Ghost
selftext:
In the aftermath of controversy and review bombing of Big Walk, over minimal AI usage disclosure, there are conflicting view points emerging from within the anti-AI community.

While the traditionalists are celebrating the negativity surrounding all of this, some people from within the anti-AI community are calling out the overblown and unwarranted response towards Big Walk.

I cannot help but feel these fractures may push anti-AI community to introspect itself, and recognize that blind bashing of AI is doing more harm than good for the overall gaming community.

Hopefully, this episode will turn at least some extremists of anti-AI community into moderates!

And, it also has the potential to bring review policy changes to the Steam as well. Bashing a game just for AI use has to be taken seriously by Steam, and if it leads to a feature, where developer can report such reviews to Steam, that will be a big positive out of all of this.

What's your view on this?

replies.author: SimoneNonvelodico

I'm not sure how it should be regulated, per se, and am very sceptical of what governments populated by old out of touch idiots who listen more to industry lobbyists than their own voters anyway tend to do as "regulation" of technology.

There definitely needs to be a change in how our economy works if any of this is to go well. You can't keep having a normal capitalist economy if labour itself has also become owned capital.

But the problem is IMO the complete rejection of the idea of the tech being potentially useful in the name of trying to make the hype die out (a lost battle) or because you feel like it's tainted by original sin. I mean, suppose the worst shit starts happening, massive collapse of employment, techno-feudalism, dystopian panopticon. How are you going to defend yourself from any of it if you're unwilling to understand or touch AI, rather than figure out how to twist it to your ends? The "resistance" in such a world would be cyberpunk hackers wielding unsanctioned hardware and tons of abliterated open/stolen models, not purists who think neural networks are ontologically evil.

replies.author: SimoneNonvelodico
replies.body:
Absolutely, the problem IMO is thinking any of this is made better by indie game dev teams refusing to dirty themselves with it.

It's an industry worth *trillions* from venture capital and major corporate customers. They have defence contracts. They are participating and orchestrating massive operations to rewrite or correct all of the world's software infrastructure to fix the exploits they themselves have uncovered. They have solved major open math problems and are now tackling physics and biology too. The biggest effect of refusing to touch it at all is that you personally remain ignorant of it and keep believing the myth that it's all hype that will deflate... other than that, nothing. Like if someone went "we only used the Pi coding agents and DeepSeek models on OpenCloud for our coding because we don't want to give money to OpenAI or Anthropic or Google", honestly I'd be like, you know what, based, makes sense. That would be a reasonable principled stance even though your money would be a tiny drop in the bucket anyway. If you want to not use it at all for a commercial project, ok. But reacting as if its use taints everything and is an unforgivable betrayal is honestly deranged. It's everywhere no matter what, and if your whole thing was wanting to fight AI as effectively as possible... you'd actually have to do it with AI too, already, or you would be hopelessly outclassed. It's like expecting an environmentalist candidate to never use a car or plane lest they're hypocritical.

replies.author: SimoneNonvelodico

The devs of this game called Big Walk went really hard on being themselves opposed to AI, disclosed nothing on Steam, made it all by hand. Then at an award they disclosed one single example of use (that was outside of Steam's disclosure policy): they apparently encountered a particularly obstinate bug in Unity, they contacted the Unity devs, no one could solve it, and so finally they just sicced AI on it and it was solved immediately.

This made a lot of judges at the award horribly conflicted about whether this game that everyone otherwise loved should even be admitted, and plenty of people started flipping out that a drop of shit in a cake makes the whole cake shit. It turned into a bigger thing because some people argued it's ok if it's coding and then this was met with a series of takes that coding is art too and so on so forth.

It's honestly pretty absurd, because I can't imagine a tinier, more forgivable "offence" and it's still elicited an incredibly violent reaction. At this point future developers just know to lie, because there is no winning when your public is this intransigent.

comments.author: NucciDev
comments.body:
I use AI to help with writing code, learning C# and Unity, and fixing bugs. I think people need to better understand the difference between AI-generated art and using AI as a tool to improve a developer's workflow.

Not all AI usage is the same, and treating it all as equally bad doesn't help anyone, especially indie developers.

Even when AI is used for art, I don't think harassment or review bombing is warranted. It's perfectly reasonable to criticize AI-generated content or choose not to support a game because of it, but that doesn't justify attacking developers.

I think the bigger issue is transparency. Developers should be honest with consumers about how AI was used, but they shouldn't be automatically condemned just for using it.

comments.author: Aggravating-Vehicle9
comments.body:
Something I've learned from AI development:

AI can do stuff for you, but it will take the shortest possible path to get feature X implemented; even if the way it did it completely messes up the overall architecture and files in the face of well-established game design and architectural principles. Put simply, AI don't give a f***.

But, that's where the human comes in. AI-defined game development isn't a case of everybody gets to be Shigeru Miyamoto and just paint big-brush-stroke high-concept imahges - you still have to care about stuff... in fact you have to care about little stuff and give very detailed architercural directions.

You have to be really engaged with the process and think about how your game will work. What kinds of systems need to exist? What components make that system? How do they compose? What tools need to exist before you can start making that stuff. 

Anybody who just telling computers to make them random crap is just vibe-coding and that will put a limit on what they can achieve. Fun games that produce unexpected, interesting gameplay are about making composable re-usable gameplay systems, and I think that's impossible without human direction. 

I could go on at length about how to get AIs on board with the scheme if anybody is interested?
